decks.title: Remainder and Factor Theorems — Part 1: The remainder theorem and the factor theorem
goals: Divide a polynomial by a linear expression and write dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder
Find a remainder without long division, using the remainder theorem
Find unknown coefficients when remainders are given
Use the factor theorem to test whether a linear expression is a factor

slides.heading: Remainder and Factor Theorems, Part 1
slides.body_md: Dividing a polynomial by $(x - a)$ leaves a remainder you can find without dividing: it is the value of the polynomial at $x = a$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed minus 3 x squared minus 6 x plus 8, crossing the x-axis at minus 2, 1 and 4; the marked point at x equals 3 has height minus 10, the remainder when the polynomial is divided by x minus 3.
visual.caption: The remainder on division by $(x - 3)$ is the height of the graph at $x = 3$: $f(3) = -10$.

slides.narration: Welcome to the remainder and factor theorems. Look at the graph. When this cubic is divided by x minus three, the remainder is minus ten, and minus ten is exactly the height of the graph at x equals three. Where the graph meets the x axis, the remainder is zero, and that gives a factor. In this part you will see why.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Divide a polynomial by a **linear expression**
Find a **remainder** quickly with the **remainder theorem**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we see what happens when a polynomial is divided by a linear expression. Then we find remainders without long division, use remainders to find missing coefficients, and finally test whether an expression is a factor.

slides.heading: Dividing by a linear expression
slides.body_md: Long division of a polynomial by $(x - a)$ gives a quotient $q(x)$ and a remainder $r$. Because the divisor has degree $1$, the remainder is a **constant**.

visual.alt: Table of the long division of 2 x cubed minus 3 x squared plus 4 x minus 5 by x minus 2 in three steps: quotient terms 2 x squared, then x, then 6; after the last subtraction the remainder is 7.
visual.caption: Quotient $2x^2 + x + 6$, remainder $7$: $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5 = (x - 2)(2x^2 + x + 6) + 7$.

slides.narration: Long division of polynomials works like long division of numbers. Divide the leading terms, multiply back, subtract, and repeat. We stop when what is left has a smaller degree than the divisor. A linear divisor always leaves a constant. Here the quotient is two x squared plus x plus six, and the remainder is seven.

slides.heading: The remainder theorem
slides.body_md: When $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - a)$, the remainder is $f(a)$. **Why:** put $x = a$ in $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$; the first term becomes $0$, so $f(a) = r$.

headers: Value of $f(x)$ at the zero of the divisor

visual.alt: Table for f of x equals 2 x cubed minus 3 x squared plus 4 x minus 5: dividing by x minus 2, x minus 1, x plus 1 and x plus 3 leaves remainders 7, minus 2, minus 14 and minus 98, exactly the values f of 2, f of 1, f of minus 1 and f of minus 3.
visual.caption: Long division and substitution give the same remainder every time.

slides.narration: Here is the shortcut. Write the division as f of x equals x minus a, times the quotient, plus the remainder. Now put x equal to a. The bracket becomes zero, so everything vanishes except the remainder. The table checks this four times: long division and substitution always agree.

slides.heading: Quick check: a remainder
slides.body_md: Substitute the value that makes the divisor zero.
slides.narration: Which value makes x minus one equal to zero? Substitute it into the polynomial carefully.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: dividing by (x + 3)
slides.body_md: Find the remainder when $x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x + 5$ is divided by $(x + 3)$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed plus 4 x squared minus 3 x plus 5 for x from minus 5 to 2, with the point at x equals minus 3 marked at height 23, the remainder on division by x plus 3.
visual.caption: At $x = -3$ the graph is at height $23$: the remainder.

slides.narration: The divisor is x plus three, which is zero when x is minus three. So we substitute minus three. Take care with the signs: minus three cubed is minus twenty seven, and four times nine is thirty six. The total is twenty three. Long division gives the same remainder, but with much more work.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dividing by (2x − 1)
slides.body_md: Find the remainder when $4x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + 1$ is divided by $(2x - 1)$.

visual.alt: Table of the value to substitute: for x minus 4 use 4; for x plus 3 use minus 3; for 2 x minus 1 use one half; for 3 x plus 2 use minus two thirds.
visual.caption: Substitute the value of $x$ that makes the divisor zero.

slides.narration: When the divisor is two x minus one, do not substitute one. Put the divisor equal to zero: two x minus one equals zero gives x equals one half. So the remainder is f of one half, which works out to five halves. The table shows the value to use for other divisors.

slides.heading: Quick check: which value?
slides.body_md: Put the divisor equal to $0$.
slides.narration: Solve x plus five equals zero. That value goes into the polynomial.

slides.heading: Finding an unknown coefficient
slides.body_md: If a remainder is given, write the remainder theorem with the unknown, and solve the equation.

nodes.label: Simplify to linear equations in the unknowns

visual.alt: Flow chart for unknown coefficients: each given factor x minus a gives f of a equals zero; each given remainder R gives f of a equals R; simplify to linear equations; solve them, simultaneously if there are two; substitute back to check.
visual.caption: One condition for each unknown.

slides.narration: Sometimes a coefficient is missing and the remainder is given instead. Substitute the zero of the divisor, keeping the unknown as a letter. You get an expression for the remainder. Set it equal to the given remainder and solve. With two unknowns, you need two conditions, and you solve them together.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: one unknown
slides.body_md: When $x^3 + kx^2 - 7x + 4$ is divided by $(x - 2)$, the remainder is $6$. Find $k$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed plus 2 x squared minus 7 x plus 4, the polynomial with k equal to 2, passing through the marked point with x equal to 2 and height 6, the given remainder.
visual.caption: With $k = 2$ the graph passes through $(2, 6)$: the remainder is $6$.

slides.narration: Substitute two, keeping k as a letter. Eight plus four k minus fourteen plus four simplifies to four k minus two. The remainder must be six, so four k minus two equals six. That gives k equals two. The graph of the finished polynomial passes through the point two, six.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: two unknowns
slides.body_md: The polynomial $x^3 + px^2 + qx - 6$ leaves remainder $8$ when divided by $(x - 2)$, and $-4$ when divided by $(x + 1)$. Find $p$ and $q$.

visual.alt: Table turning each condition into an equation: dividing by x minus 2 leaves 8, which gives 2 p plus q equals 3; dividing by x plus 1 leaves minus 4, which gives p minus q equals 3.
visual.caption: Two conditions give two linear equations in $p$ and $q$.

slides.narration: Each condition gives one equation. Substituting two gives two p plus q equals three. Substituting minus one gives p minus q equals three. Add the equations to remove q: three p equals six, so p is two. Then q is minus one. Always substitute back to check both remainders.

slides.heading: The factor theorem
slides.body_md: $(x - a)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$. A zero of the graph at $x = a$ means a factor $(x - a)$; a zero at $x = \dfrac{b}{c}$ means a factor $(cx - b)$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals 2 x cubed minus x squared minus 7 x plus 6, crossing the x-axis at minus 2, 1 and 1.5; the factors are x plus 2, x minus 1 and 2 x minus 3.
visual.caption: Each zero gives a factor: $-2 \to (x + 2)$, $1 \to (x - 1)$, $\dfrac{3}{2} \to (2x - 3)$.

slides.narration: If the remainder is zero, the divisor goes in exactly, so it is a factor. That is the factor theorem: x minus a is a factor exactly when f of a is zero. On the graph, each crossing of the x axis gives a factor. A crossing at three halves gives the factor two x minus three.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: testing factors
slides.body_md: Test whether $(x - 3)$ and $(x + 1)$ are factors of $x^3 - 2x^2 - 2x - 3$.

visual.alt: Table testing two expressions for f of x equals x cubed minus 2 x squared minus 2 x minus 3: at x equals 3 the value is 0, so x minus 3 is a factor; at x equals minus 1 the value is minus 4, so x plus 1 is not a factor.
visual.caption: Value $0$ means a factor; any other value is the remainder.

slides.narration: Test each expression separately. For x minus three, substitute three: the value is zero, so it is a factor. For x plus one, substitute minus one: the value is minus four, so it is not a factor, and minus four is the remainder. Dividing by x minus three leaves x squared plus x plus one.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the factor
slides.body_md: Try the values that make each expression zero.
slides.narration: Add up the coefficients. What does that tell you about x minus one?

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a factor (2x + 3)
slides.body_md: Show that $(2x + 3)$ is a factor of $2x^3 + 5x^2 - x - 6$.
bullets: **Conclusion —** the value is $0$, so $(2x + 3)$ is a factor: $2x^3 + 5x^2 - x - 6 = (2x + 3)(x^2 + x - 2)$.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals 2 x cubed plus 5 x squared minus x minus 6, crossing the x-axis at minus 2, minus 1.5 and 1; the zero minus 1.5 matches the factor 2 x plus 3.
visual.caption: The zero $-\dfrac{3}{2}$ matches the factor $(2x + 3)$.

slides.narration: Put two x plus three equal to zero: x is minus three halves. Substitute carefully, cubing and squaring the fraction first. The terms add up to zero, so two x plus three is a factor. The graph crosses the x axis at minus one and a half, as expected.

slides.heading: Remainder or factor?
slides.body_md: One substitution answers both questions: the value $f(a)$ is the remainder, and if it is $0$, $(x - a)$ is a factor.

headers: and the graph of $y = f(x)$ at $x = a$…
rows: is at height $f(a)$, off the axis
leaves no remainder: $(x - a)$ is a factor

visual.alt: Table linking the two theorems: if f of a is not zero, dividing by x minus a leaves the remainder f of a and the graph is off the axis at a; if f of a is zero, x minus a is a factor and the graph meets the x-axis at a.
visual.caption: The factor theorem is the remainder theorem with remainder $0$.

slides.narration: The two theorems work together. Substitute the zero of the divisor. If the answer is not zero, it is the remainder, and the graph is off the axis there. If the answer is zero, the divisor is a factor, and the graph meets the axis. The factor theorem is simply the remainder theorem with remainder zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: which factor?
slides.body_md: Which value of $x$ makes $(x + 2)$ zero?
slides.narration: Remember: x minus a goes with f of a. Which expression goes with f of two?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$; a linear divisor leaves a constant remainder
Remainder on division by $(x - a)$ is $f(a)$; by $(ax + b)$ it is $f\left(-\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$
Given remainders: one equation per condition
$(x - a)$ is a factor exactly when $f(a) = 0$

rows: remainder on division by $(x - a)$ is $f(a)$; by $(ax + b)$ it is $f\left(-\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$
remainder in terms of $k$ = given remainder
$(x - a)$ is a factor exactly when $f(a) = 0$

visual.alt: Summary table for part 1: division gives f of x equals x minus a times q of x plus r; the remainder theorem; finding unknown coefficients; the factor theorem.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. Dividing by a linear expression leaves a constant remainder. The remainder theorem finds it by substituting the zero of the divisor. A given remainder gives an equation for an unknown coefficient. And when the value is zero, the factor theorem tells you the divisor is a factor.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Mistake:** sign slips with negative values: $(-2)^2 = 4$ but $(-2)^3 = -8$
**Mistake:** saying "factor" when the value is not $0$
slides.narration: Always write the value you substitute and show each term, because the first mark is for the substitution. Put the divisor equal to zero to find that value. Watch the signs when you cube a negative number. And only call an expression a factor when the value is exactly zero; otherwise it is the remainder.

decks.title: Remainder and Factor Theorems — Part 2: Unknown coefficients and factorising cubics completely
goals: Find unknown coefficients when one or two factors are given
Find a factor of a cubic by trial
Divide and factorise a cubic polynomial completely
Recognise a quadratic factor that cannot be factorised further, and check a factorisation

slides.heading: Remainder and Factor Theorems, Part 2
slides.body_md: A cubic with three zeros splits into three linear factors. The factor theorem finds the first one.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed plus x squared minus 10 x plus 8, crossing the x-axis at minus 4, 1 and 2, so it factorises as x plus 4, times x minus 1, times x minus 2.
visual.caption: Three zeros, three linear factors: $(x + 4)(x - 1)(x - 2)$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. This cubic meets the x axis three times, at minus four, one and two, so it splits into three linear factors. In this part you will find missing coefficients from given factors, and learn to factorise any cubic in the syllabus completely, starting from a single trial value.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Recognise a quadratic that **cannot be factorised further**, and **check** your answer
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We use the factor theorem to find missing coefficients. Then we factorise cubics: try a value, divide, and factorise what is left. Finally we learn to check an answer quickly.

slides.heading: Unknown coefficients from factors
slides.body_md: A given factor $(x - a)$ means $f(a) = 0$. Each factor or remainder gives one equation; two unknowns need two conditions.

nodes.label: Simplify to linear equations in the unknowns

visual.alt: Flow chart for unknown coefficients: each given factor x minus a gives f of a equals zero; each given remainder R gives f of a equals R; simplify to linear equations; solve them, simultaneously if there are two; substitute back to check.
visual.caption: One condition for each unknown.

slides.narration: If x minus a is a factor, then f of a is zero. That gives an equation in the unknown coefficient. With two unknowns, you need two conditions, either two factors, or a factor and a remainder. Each gives a linear equation, and you solve the pair simultaneously.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: find k, then factorise
slides.body_md: Find $k$ if $(x + 2)$ is a factor of $2x^3 + kx^2 - 13x - 6$, and factorise the polynomial completely.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals 2 x cubed minus x squared minus 13 x minus 6, crossing the x-axis at minus 2, minus 0.5 and 3, matching the factors x plus 2, 2 x plus 1 and x minus 3.
visual.caption: With $k = -1$: zeros $-2$, $-\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $3$.

slides.narration: Since x plus two is a factor, f of minus two is zero. Keep k as a letter: the value simplifies to four k plus four, so k is minus one. Now divide by x plus two. The quotient is two x squared minus five x minus three, which splits as two x plus one, times x minus three.

slides.heading: Quick check: find k
slides.narration: Substitute two, keep k as a letter, and set the result equal to zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two factors given
slides.body_md: Both $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 3)$ are factors of $x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 12$. Find $a$ and $b$, and the third factor.

visual.alt: Table for two given factors: x minus 2 gives f of 2 equals 0, that is 2 a plus b equals 2; x plus 3 gives f of minus 3 equals 0, that is 3 a minus b equals 13; adding gives a equals 3 and b equals minus 4.
visual.caption: Two factors, two equations, two unknowns.

slides.narration: Each factor gives an equation. From f of two equals zero, two a plus b equals two. From f of minus three equals zero, three a minus b equals thirteen. Adding them gives five a equals fifteen, so a is three and b is minus four. The polynomial then factorises with a third factor, x plus two.

slides.heading: Factorising a cubic completely
slides.body_md: Find one zero $a$ by trial, divide by $(x - a)$, then factorise the quadratic quotient.

nodes.label: Try divisors of the constant term (and fractions if the leading coefficient is not $1$)
Find $a$ with $f(a) = 0$: $(x - a)$ is a factor
Check by expanding or by a value

visual.alt: Flow chart for factorising a cubic completely: try divisors of the constant term; find a value a that makes f of a zero, so x minus a is a factor; divide to get a quadratic quotient; factorise the quotient; check by expanding or by substituting a value.
visual.caption: Trial, divide, factorise, check.

slides.narration: Here is the method for any cubic in the syllabus. Try small values that divide the constant term until the polynomial is zero. That value gives one factor. Divide by it to get a quadratic. Then factorise the quadratic by splitting the middle term. Finally, check your answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: trial, then divide
slides.body_md: Factorise $x^3 - 3x^2 - 10x + 24$ completely.

visual.alt: Trial table for x cubed minus 3 x squared minus 10 x plus 24: at 1 the value is 12, at minus 1 it is 30, at 2 it is 0, so x minus 2 is a factor.
visual.caption: Try $\pm 1$, $\pm 2$, … (divisors of $24$) until the value is $0$.

slides.narration: The constant term is twenty four, so try its divisors. One gives twelve, minus one gives thirty, but two gives zero. So x minus two is a factor. Dividing leaves x squared minus x minus twelve, which factorises as x minus four, times x plus three.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: long division
slides.body_md: Factorise $2x^3 - 3x^2 - 17x + 30$ completely.

visual.alt: Table of the long division of 2 x cubed minus 3 x squared minus 17 x plus 30 by x minus 2: quotient terms 2 x squared, then x, then minus 15; the remainder is 0.
visual.caption: Quotient $2x^2 + x - 15$, remainder $0$.

slides.narration: One gives twelve, but two gives zero, so x minus two is a factor. The table shows the long division: divide the leading terms, multiply back and subtract, three times. The quotient is two x squared plus x minus fifteen, which splits as x plus three, times two x minus five.

slides.heading: Quick check: where to start
slides.body_md: Which values could be zeros?
slides.narration: Think about which numbers can divide the constant term.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a quadratic that will not split
slides.body_md: Factorise $x^3 + x^2 - 4x + 6$ as far as possible.
bullets: **Step 3 —** for $x^2 - 2x + 2$: $(-2)^2 - 4 \times 1 \times 2 = -4 < 0$, so it has no linear factors.

visual.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed plus x squared minus 4 x plus 6, crossing the x-axis only once, at minus 3; the quadratic factor x squared minus 2 x plus 2 is never zero.
visual.caption: Only one zero: the quadratic factor $x^2 - 2x + 2$ cannot be factorised further.

slides.narration: Trying values, only minus three gives zero, so x plus three is a factor. Dividing leaves x squared minus two x plus two. Its discriminant is negative, so it has no real zeros and no linear factors. The graph agrees: it crosses the axis only once. We stop here.

slides.heading: Choosing trial values
slides.body_md: A few quick tests tell you where to start.

rows: Coefficients of even powers and of odd powers have equal sums
try the divisors of the constant term
also try fractions $\dfrac{p}{q}$, $q$ dividing the leading coefficient

visual.alt: Table of clues for trial values: if the coefficients add up to zero, x minus 1 is a factor; if the even-power and odd-power coefficients have equal sums, x plus 1 is a factor; with leading coefficient 1 try divisors of the constant term; otherwise also try fractions.
visual.caption: Quick tests save time in the exam.

slides.narration: Before trying values at random, use the clues. If the coefficients add up to zero, x minus one is a factor. If the even power coefficients and the odd power coefficients have the same sum, x plus one is a factor. Otherwise try the divisors of the constant term, and fractions when the leading coefficient is not one.

slides.heading: Quick check: the other two factors
slides.body_md: Divide, then factorise the quadratic.
slides.narration: Divide by x plus one, then find two numbers for the quadratic.

slides.heading: Checking a factorisation
slides.body_md: Substitute easy values such as $x = 0, 1, -1$ into the polynomial and into your product of factors: they must agree.

visual.alt: Table checking the factorisation of 2 x cubed minus 3 x squared minus 17 x plus 30 at x equals 0, 1 and minus 1: the polynomial and the product of factors both give 30, 12 and 42.
visual.caption: A quick value check catches sign slips.

slides.narration: Always check. Put x equal to zero, one and minus one in the original polynomial and in your factors. The numbers must match. At zero, the product of the constant terms of the factors must equal the constant term. A mismatch shows a sign slip at once.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Think about what $f(1)$ is.
slides.narration: What do you get when you put x equal to one in any polynomial?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Given factor $(x - a)$: $f(a) = 0$; two unknowns need two conditions
Factorise a cubic: trial value, divide, factorise the quadratic
Trial values divide the constant term; fractions if the leading coefficient is not $1$
A quadratic with negative discriminant cannot be factorised further

rows: two conditions give two linear equations; solve simultaneously
trial, divide, factorise the quadratic quotient
stop: it cannot be factorised further

visual.alt: Summary table for part 2: find k from a factor with f of a equal to zero; two unknowns from two conditions; factorise a cubic by trial, division and factorising the quadratic; stop when the quotient has no real zeros; check by expanding or by values.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. A given factor gives f of a equals zero, an equation for an unknown. To factorise a cubic, find one zero by trial, divide, and factorise the quadratic quotient. Stop if the quadratic has no real zeros. Always check your answer with simple values.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Factorise a cubic (3 marks):** trial value 1 + quotient 1 + complete factorisation 1
**Mistake:** stopping at $(x - a)\times$ quadratic when the quadratic still factorises
**Mistake:** sign errors in the quotient: check by expanding
**Mistake:** writing roots such as $x = 2$ instead of factors such as $(x - 2)$
**Mistake:** a factor such as $(2x - 5)$ written as $\left(x - \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$ without the 2
slides.narration: Show the trial value that gives zero, the division, and the final product of factors: each earns a mark. Do not stop at a quadratic factor that still splits. Give factors, not roots. And if a zero is a fraction such as five halves, write the factor as two x minus five, so the product still equals the polynomial.

notes.title: Factorisation of Polynomials: Remainder and Factor Theorems — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Dividing a polynomial by a linear expression
sections.body_md:
- **Division algorithm:** dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, that is $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$.
- The remainder has a smaller degree than the divisor, so on division by a linear expression it is a **constant**.
- Long division: divide the leading terms, multiply back, subtract; repeat until the remainder is a constant.

*Example:* $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5 = (x - 2)(2x^2 + x + 6) + 7$.

This chapter uses polynomials of degree up to $3$ only; polynomials of degree higher than $3$ are not in the ICSE 2027 syllabus.

key_terms.definition_md: What is left after dividing; for a linear divisor it is a constant.

visual.alt: Table of the long division of 2 x cubed minus 3 x squared plus 4 x minus 5 by x minus 2 in three steps: quotient terms 2 x squared, then x, then 6; after the last subtraction the remainder is 7.
visual.caption: Quotient $2x^2 + x + 6$, remainder $7$: $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5 = (x - 2)(2x^2 + x + 6) + 7$.

sections.heading: 2. The remainder theorem
sections.body_md:
When $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - a)$, the **remainder is $f(a)$**. Put $x = a$ in $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$: the first term becomes $0$.

- Divisor $(x + a)$: remainder $f(-a)$.
- Divisor $(ax + b)$: remainder $f\left(-\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$; divisor $(ax - b)$: remainder $f\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$.
- Rule: **put the divisor equal to $0$** and substitute that value.

*Example:* $x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x + 5$ divided by $(x + 3)$: $f(-3) = -27 + 36 + 9 + 5 = 23$.

key_terms.definition_md: The remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - a)$ is $f(a)$.
The value of $x$ that makes the divisor $0$; for $2x - 1$ it is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

headers: Value of $f(x)$ at the zero of the divisor

visual.alt: Table for f of x equals 2 x cubed minus 3 x squared plus 4 x minus 5: dividing by x minus 2, x minus 1, x plus 1 and x plus 3 leaves remainders 7, minus 2, minus 14 and minus 98, exactly the values f of 2, f of 1, f of minus 1 and f of minus 3.
visual.caption: Long division and substitution give the same remainder every time.

visuals.alt: Table of the value to substitute: for x minus 4 use 4; for x plus 3 use minus 3; for 2 x minus 1 use one half; for 3 x plus 2 use minus two thirds.
visuals.caption: Substitute the value of $x$ that makes the divisor zero.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed plus 4 x squared minus 3 x plus 5 for x from minus 5 to 2, with the point at x equals minus 3 marked at height 23, the remainder on division by x plus 3.
visuals.caption: At $x = -3$ the graph is at height $23$: the remainder.

sections.heading: 3. Unknown coefficients from given remainders
sections.body_md:
1. Substitute the zero of each divisor, keeping the unknowns as letters.
2. Set each result equal to the given remainder: one **linear equation** per condition.
3. Solve (simultaneously for two unknowns) and substitute back to check.

*Examples:* $x^3 + kx^2 - 7x + 4$ leaves $6$ on division by $(x - 2)$: $4k - 2 = 6$, so $k = 2$. Equal remainders: set the two remainders equal to each other.

key_terms.definition_md: A given remainder or factor; each gives one equation in the unknowns.

formulas.label: Remainder R on division by x − a

nodes.label: Simplify to linear equations in the unknowns

visual.alt: Flow chart for unknown coefficients: each given factor x minus a gives f of a equals zero; each given remainder R gives f of a equals R; simplify to linear equations; solve them, simultaneously if there are two; substitute back to check.
visual.caption: One condition for each unknown.

visuals.alt: Table turning each condition into an equation: dividing by x minus 2 leaves 8, which gives 2 p plus q equals 3; dividing by x plus 1 leaves minus 4, which gives p minus q equals 3.
visuals.caption: Two conditions give two linear equations in $p$ and $q$.

visuals.alt: Graph of y equals x cubed plus 2 x squared minus 7 x plus 4, the polynomial with k equal to 2, passing through the marked point with x equal to 2 and height 6, the given remainder.
visuals.caption: With $k = 2$ the graph passes through $(2, 6)$: the remainder is $6$.

sections.heading: 4. The factor theorem
sections.body_md:
$(x - a)$ is a **factor** of $f(x)$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$ (the remainder theorem with remainder $0$).

- $f(-a) = 0 \iff (x + a)$ is a factor; $f\left(\dfrac{b}{c}\right) = 0 \iff (cx - b)$ is a factor.
- A zero of $f$ is where the graph of $y = f(x)$ meets the $x$-axis: each zero gives a factor.
- If $f(a) \ne 0$, then $(x - a)$ is not a factor and $f(a)$ is the remainder.

key_terms.definition_md: $(x - a)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ if and only if $f(a) = 0$.

sections.heading: 5. Unknown coefficients from given factors
sections.body_md:
- One factor $(x - a)$ and one unknown: solve $f(a) = 0$.
- Two unknowns: use two conditions (two factors, or a factor and a remainder) and solve the two linear equations together.
- A divisor such as $x^2 - x - 2$ is the product $(x - 2)(x + 1)$: use $f(2) = 0$ and $f(-1) = 0$.

*Example:* $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 3)$ are factors of $x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 12$: $2a + b = 2$ and $3a - b = 13$, so $a = 3$, $b = -4$.

sections.heading: 6. Factorising a cubic completely
sections.body_md:
1. **Trial:** try divisors of the constant term ($\pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$); if the leading coefficient is not $1$, also try fractions $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with $q$ dividing it.
2. When $f(a) = 0$, $(x - a)$ is a factor. **Divide** (long division or by inspection): $f(x) = (x - a)q(x)$.
3. **Factorise the quadratic** $q(x)$ by splitting the middle term.
4. If $q(x)$ has a negative discriminant, it **cannot be factorised further**.

*Example:* $x^3 - 3x^2 - 10x + 24$: $f(2) = 0$, quotient $x^2 - x - 12$, so $(x - 2)(x - 4)(x + 3)$.

sections.heading: 7. Quick tests and checking
sections.body_md:
- Sum of coefficients $= 0$: $f(1) = 0$, so $(x - 1)$ is a factor.
- Sum of coefficients of even powers $=$ sum of coefficients of odd powers: $f(-1) = 0$, so $(x + 1)$ is a factor.
- **Check** a factorisation by expanding, or by comparing values at $x = 0, 1, -1$.
- Give the answer as **factors**, e.g. $(2x - 5)$, not as roots such as $x = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Remainder (2 marks):* value substituted 1; remainder 1.
- *Unknown coefficient (3 marks):* remainder or factor written in terms of $k$ 1; equation 1; value 1.
- *Two unknowns (4 marks):* each equation 1 + 1; solving 1; values 1.
- *Factorise a cubic (3–4 marks):* trial value giving $0$ 1; quotient 1; complete factorisation 1 (+ 1 for showing the division).
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Substituting $a$ instead of $-a$ for the divisor $(x + a)$, or $1$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $(2x - 1)$.
2. Sign slips with negative values: $(-3)^2 = 9$ but $(-3)^3 = -27$.
3. Calling an expression a factor when the value is not $0$.
4. Stopping with a quadratic factor that still factorises.
5. Errors in the quotient: check by expanding.
6. Writing roots instead of factors, or $\left(x - \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$ instead of $(2x - 5)$.

cards.front_md: State the **division algorithm** for dividing $f(x)$ by $(x - a)$.
cards.back_md: $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$, where $q(x)$ is the quotient and $r$ the remainder.

cards.front_md: Why is the remainder a constant when the divisor is linear?
cards.back_md: The remainder always has a smaller degree than the divisor, and the divisor has degree $1$.

cards.front_md: State the **remainder theorem**.
cards.back_md: When $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - a)$, the remainder is $f(a)$.

cards.front_md: Remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x + 4)$?
Remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(3x - 2)$?
cards.back_md: $f\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$: put $3x - 2 = 0$.

cards.front_md: Remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(ax + b)$?
cards.back_md: $f\left(-\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$.

cards.front_md: Remainder when $x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x + 5$ is divided by $(x + 3)$?
How do you find $k$ when the remainder is given?
cards.back_md: Substitute the zero of the divisor keeping $k$, set the result equal to the given remainder, and solve.

cards.front_md: Two unknown coefficients: how many conditions do you need?
cards.back_md: Two; each gives a linear equation, and you solve them simultaneously.

cards.front_md: Two polynomials leave the **same remainder** on division by $(x - a)$. What equation do you write?
cards.back_md: Set their values at $x = a$ equal: $f(a) = g(a)$.

cards.front_md: State the **factor theorem**.
cards.back_md: $(x - a)$ is a factor of $f(x)$ exactly when $f(a) = 0$.

cards.front_md: If $f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = 0$, which factor does $f(x)$ have?
If $f(-5) = 0$, which factor does $f(x)$ have?
What does a zero of $f$ look like on the graph of $y = f(x)$?
cards.back_md: A point where the graph meets the $x$-axis.

cards.front_md: Is $(x + 1)$ a factor of $x^3 - 2x^2 - 2x - 3$?
cards.back_md: No: $f(-1) = -4$, which is the remainder.

cards.front_md: The coefficients of $f(x)$ add up to $0$. Which factor must it have?
cards.back_md: $(x - 1)$, because $f(1)$ is the sum of the coefficients.

cards.front_md: When is $(x + 1)$ a factor, by a quick test?
cards.back_md: When the coefficients of even powers and of odd powers have equal sums.

cards.front_md: $(x - 3)$ is a factor of $2x^3 - 5x^2 + kx - 6$. Find $k$.
A cubic is divisible by $x^2 - x - 2$. Which two values make it zero?
Which values do you try first when factorising $x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c$?
cards.back_md: The divisors of the constant term $c$.

cards.front_md: Leading coefficient not $1$: which extra trial values?
cards.back_md: Fractions $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with $p$ dividing the constant term and $q$ dividing the leading coefficient.

cards.front_md: Three steps to factorise a cubic completely?
cards.back_md: Find a zero by trial; divide by the matching factor; factorise the quadratic quotient.

cards.front_md: Factorise $x^3 - 3x^2 - 10x + 24$.
Factorise $2x^3 - 3x^2 - 17x + 30$.
When do you stop factorising a quadratic quotient?
cards.back_md: When its discriminant is negative: it has no linear factors, e.g. $x^2 - 2x + 2$.

cards.front_md: Factorise $x^3 + x^2 - 4x + 6$ as far as possible.
How can you check a factorisation quickly?
cards.back_md: Compare the polynomial and the product of factors at $x = 0$, $1$ and $-1$.

cards.front_md: A zero is $\dfrac{5}{2}$. How do you write the factor?
cards.back_md: $(2x - 5)$, not $\left(x - \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$ alone, so the product still equals the polynomial.

questions.stem_md: According to the remainder theorem, when a polynomial $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - a)$, the remainder is
questions.solution_md: Write $f(x) = (x - a)q(x) + r$ and put $x = a$: the first term becomes $0$, so $r = f(a)$. For example, $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5$ divided by $(x - 2)$ leaves $7$, which is $f(2)$; $f(-2) = -41$.

questions.stem_md: What is the remainder when $x^3 - 5x^2 + 2x + 9$ is divided by $(x - 1)$?
questions.solution_md: Put $x = 1$: $f(1) = 1^3 - 5 \times 1^2 + 2 \times 1 + 9 = 1 - 5 + 2 + 9 = 7$. Option (c) is $f(-1)$, and (d) is only the constant term, $f(0)$.

questions.stem_md: To find the remainder when $3x^3 + x^2 - 4x + 2$ is divided by $(3x + 1)$ using the remainder theorem, which value of $x$ should be substituted?
questions.solution_md: Substitute the value that makes the divisor zero: $3x + 1 = 0$ gives $x = -\dfrac{1}{3}$, so the remainder is $f\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$. Option (d) has the wrong sign; (b) inverts the fraction.

questions.stem_md: Find the remainder when $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 5x - 4$ is divided by $(2x - 1)$.
questions.solution_md: $2x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, and $f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 - 3 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + 5 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - 4 = \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{5}{2} - 4 = -2$. Option (a) substitutes $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, (b) substitutes $x = 1$ and (c) substitutes $x = 2$.

questions.stem_md: When $x^3 + kx^2 - 2x + 1$ is divided by $(x + 2)$, the remainder is $5$. What is the value of $k$?
questions.solution_md: $f(-2) = (-2)^3 + k \times (-2)^2 - 2 \times (-2) + 1 = -8 + 4k + 4 + 1 = 4k - 3$, so $4k - 3 = 5$ and $k = 2$. Option (b) comes from substituting $x = 2$ instead of $x = -2$.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a factor of $x^3 - 3x^2 - 6x + 8$?
questions.solution_md: The coefficients add up to $1 - 3 - 6 + 8 = 0$, so $f(1) = 0$ and $(x - 1)$ is a factor. The others fail: $f(-1) = 10$, $f(2) = -8$ and $f(-4) = -80$.

questions.stem_md: If $(x - 3)$ is a factor of $2x^3 - 5x^2 + kx - 6$, then $k$ equals
questions.solution_md: By the factor theorem $f(3) = 0$: $f(3) = 2 \times 3^3 - 5 \times 3^2 + 3k - 6 = 54 - 45 + 3k - 6 = 3k + 3$, so $k = -1$. Option (a) comes from using $f(-3) = 0$ by mistake.

questions.stem_md: $(2x + 1)$ is a factor of a polynomial $f(x)$. Which of these statements must be true?
questions.solution_md: By the factor theorem, $(2x + 1)$ is a factor exactly when $f$ is zero at the value that makes $2x + 1 = 0$, that is $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. The others need not hold: for $f(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 + 2x + 1 = (2x + 1)(x^2 + 1)$, $f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{5}{2}$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is the complete factorisation of $3x^3 + 2x^2 - 19x + 6$?
questions.solution_md: $f(2) = 3 \times 2^3 + 2 \times 2^2 - 19 \times 2 + 6 = 24 + 8 - 38 + 6 = 0$, so $(x - 2)$ is a factor. Dividing, $3x^3 + 2x^2 - 19x + 6 = (x - 2)(3x^2 + 8x - 3) = (x - 2)(x + 3)(3x - 1)$. Expanding (b) gives the signs of every term except $x^3$ reversed.

questions.stem_md: You want to factorise $x^3 + 2x^2 - 13x + 10$ by trying values of $x$. Which values are worth trying first?
questions.solution_md: An integer zero of a polynomial with leading coefficient $1$ must divide the constant term, $10$. Trying them, $f(1) = 1^3 + 2 \times 1^2 - 13 \times 1 + 10 = 1 + 2 - 13 + 10 = 0$, so $(x - 1)$ is a factor; in fact $x^3 + 2x^2 - 13x + 10 = (x + 5)(x - 1)(x - 2)$.

questions.stem_md: The coefficients of $3x^3 - 5x^2 + 4x - 2$ add up to $0$. Which factor does this show the polynomial has?
questions.solution_md: The sum of the coefficients is $f(1)$: $3 - 5 + 4 - 2 = 0$, so $(x - 1)$ is a factor. The others are not: $f(-1) = -14$, $f\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $f(2) = 10$.

questions.stem_md: The polynomial $x^3 + ax + 4$ leaves the same remainder when divided by $(x - 1)$ as when divided by $(x + 1)$. Find $a$.
Both $(x - 1)$ and $(x + 2)$ are factors of $x^3 + px^2 + qx + 2$. What are $p$ and $q$?
questions.solution_md: $f(1) = 1 + p + q + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow p + q = -3$ and $f(-2) = -8 + 4p - 2q + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow 2p - q = 3$. Adding, $3p = 0$, so $p = 0$ and $q = -3$. Option (d) makes $f(1) = 0$ but gives $f(-2) = 6$.

questions.stem_md: One factor of $x^3 - 13x - 12$ is $(x + 1)$. What are the other two factors?
questions.solution_md: Dividing by $(x + 1)$: $x^3 - 13x - 12 = (x + 1)(x^2 - x - 12)$, and $x^2 - x - 12 = (x - 4)(x + 3)$. Option (c) has both signs reversed.

questions.stem_md: When a polynomial $f(x)$ is divided by $(x - 2)$, the quotient is $x^2 + 3x - 1$ and the remainder is $4$. What is $f(2)$?
questions.solution_md: $f(x) = (x - 2)(x^2 + 3x - 1) + 4$. At $x = 2$ the first term is $0$: $f(2) = 0 \times 9 + 4 = 4$. This is the remainder theorem. Option (d) is the value of the quotient at $x = 2$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these polynomials is exactly divisible by $(x + 1)$?
questions.solution_md: Put $x = -1$ in each. For the first, $f(-1) = (-1)^3 + 2 \times (-1)^2 + 3 \times (-1) + 2 = -1 + 2 - 3 + 2 = 0$. The others give $6$, $-4$ and $1$, so they leave remainders.

questions.stem_md: The graph of a cubic polynomial $y = f(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis only at the three marked points. Which of these is **not** a factor of $f(x)$?
questions.solution_md: The graph meets the $x$-axis where $f(x) = 0$: at $x = -1$, $3$ and $4$. So $(x + 1)$, $(x - 3)$ and $(x - 4)$ are factors. $(x + 3)$ would need $f(-3) = 0$, but the graph does not cross the axis at $-3$.

assets.alt: Graph of a cubic polynomial y equals f of x, rising from the bottom left, crossing the x-axis at the three marked points minus 1, 3 and 4, with a turning point above the axis between minus 1 and 3.
assets.caption: The cubic crosses the $x$-axis only at the marked points.

questions.stem_md: Meera found that $(x - 2)$ is a factor of $x^3 - 6x^2 + 3x + 10$. She wrote $x^3 - 6x^2 + 3x + 10 = (x - 2)(x^2 - 4x + 5)$ and said that it cannot be factorised further. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Her quotient is wrong: it should be $x^2 - 4x - 5$, which factorises as $(x - 5)(x + 1)$.
Her work is correct, because $x^2 - 4x + 5$ has no linear factors.

questions.solution_md: Expanding her product: $(x - 2)(x^2 - 4x + 5) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 13x - 10$, which is not the given polynomial. The correct division gives $x^3 - 6x^2 + 3x + 10 = (x - 2)(x^2 - 4x - 5) = (x - 2)(x + 1)(x - 5)$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The remainder when $x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 3$ is divided by $(x + 2)$ is $5$.

**Reason (R):** When a polynomial $f(x)$ is divided by $(x + a)$, the remainder is $f(-a)$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $f(-2) = (-2)^3 + 2 \times (-2)^2 - (-2) + 3 = -8 + 8 + 2 + 3 = 5$, so A is true. R is the remainder theorem for the divisor $x + a$, whose zero is $-a$, and it is exactly the rule used to get A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $(x - 2)$ is a factor of $x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 4$.

**Reason (R):** The constant term of $x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 4$ is divisible by $2$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $f(2) = 2^3 + 2^2 - 4 \times 2 - 4 = 8 + 4 - 8 - 4 = 0$, so A is true by the factor theorem. R is also true, but divisibility of the constant term only makes $2$ a value worth trying: $4$ also divides $-4$, yet $f(4) = 60$. So R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x - 6$ can be written as a product of three linear factors with integer coefficients.

**Reason (R):** $x^2 + 3$ is positive for every real value of $x$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: Grouping, $x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x - 6 = x^2(x - 2) + 3(x - 2) = (x - 2)(x^2 + 3)$. Since $x^2 + 3 \ge 3$, it is never zero and has no linear factor, so A is false. R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The remainder when $8x^3 - 4x + 3$ is divided by $(2x + 1)$ is $4$.

**Reason (R):** The remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(ax + b)$ is $f\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $f\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 8 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 - 4 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 3 = -1 + 2 + 3 = 4$, so A is true. R is false: the value to substitute is the zero of $ax + b$, which is $-\dfrac{b}{a}$. Here R would give $f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2$, not $4$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If $(x + 1)$ is a factor of $x^3 + kx^2 + x + 6$, then $k = -4$.

**Reason (R):** $(x + 1)$ is a factor of a polynomial $f(x)$ exactly when $f(-1) = 0$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $f(-1) = -1 + k - 1 + 6 = k + 4$; setting $k + 4 = 0$ gives $k = -4$. R is the factor theorem, and it is the reason A holds.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dividing $x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x - 3$ by $(x - 3)$ leaves $3$ over.

**Reason (R):** Substituting $x = a$ in a polynomial $f(x)$ gives the remainder on division by $(x - a)$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $f(3) = 3^3 - 6 \times 3^2 + 9 \times 3 - 3 = 27 - 54 + 27 - 3 = -3$, so the remainder is $-3$, not $3$: A is false. R is the remainder theorem, which is true.

questions.stem_md: If the coefficients of a polynomial $f(x)$ add up to $0$, then $(x - 1)$ is a factor of $f(x)$.
questions.solution_md: Putting $x = 1$ in $f(x)$ just adds the coefficients, so $f(1) = 0$ and the factor theorem gives the factor $(x - 1)$. For example, in $2x^3 - 5x^2 + x + 2$: $2 - 5 + 1 + 2 = 0$.

questions.stem_md: When a cubic polynomial is divided by $(x - 4)$, the remainder can be an expression of degree $1$, such as $2x + 3$.
questions.solution_md: The remainder always has a smaller degree than the divisor. $(x - 4)$ has degree $1$, so the remainder is a constant (possibly $0$).

questions.stem_md: When $x^3 - 2x + 7$ is divided by $(x + 3)$, the remainder is $-14$.
$(x + 2)$ is a factor of $x^3 + 8$.
The cubic polynomial $x^3 - x^2 - 5x - 3$ has three different linear factors.
questions.solution_md: $f(-1) = (-1)^3 - (-1)^2 - 5 \times (-1) - 3 = -1 - 1 + 5 - 3 = 0$. Dividing by $(x + 1)$ gives $x^2 - 2x - 3 = (x + 1)(x - 3)$, so $x^3 - x^2 - 5x - 3 = (x + 1)^2(x - 3)$: the factor $(x + 1)$ is repeated, and there are only two different linear factors.

questions.stem_md: If $f(2) = 0$, then $(x + 2)$ is a factor of $f(x)$.
questions.solution_md: $f(2) = 0$ makes $(x - 2)$ a factor, not $(x + 2)$. For example, $f(x) = x^3 - 8$ has $f(2) = 0$ but $f(-2) = -16$.

questions.stem_md: To find the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x + 5)$, you work out the value of $f(x)$ at $x =$ ___.
questions.solution_md: The divisor is zero when $x + 5 = 0$, that is at $x = -5$, so the remainder is $f(-5)$.

questions.stem_md: The remainder when $2x^3 - x^2 + 3$ is divided by $(x - 2)$ is ___.
If $(x - 4)$ is a factor of $x^3 - 5x^2 + kx + 8$, then $k =$ ___.
When $x^3 - 2x^2 - 9x + 18$ is factorised completely, two of its factors are $(x - 2)$ and $(x - 3)$. The third factor is ___.
questions.solution_md: Grouping: $x^3 - 2x^2 - 9x + 18 = x^2(x - 2) - 9(x - 2) = (x - 2)(x^2 - 9) = (x - 2)(x - 3)(x + 3)$. So the third factor is (x + 3).

questions.stem_md: Use the remainder theorem with the divisor $(2x - 1)$: for the polynomial $6x^3 + x^2 - 4$, the remainder is ___.
questions.solution_md: $2x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$: $f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 6 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 - 4 = \dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} - 4 = -3$.

questions.stem_md: By the factor theorem, if $f(-2) = 0$, then ___ is a factor of $f(x)$.
questions.solution_md: $x = -2$ is the zero of $x + 2$, so (x + 2) is a factor.

questions.stem_md: Without long division, calculate what is left over when $(x - 3)$ divides $x^3 - 4x^2 + 6x - 5$.
Find the remainder when $4x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 7$ is divided by $(2x + 1)$. Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution_md: $2x + 1 = 0$ gives $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$, and $f\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 4 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 + 2 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 - \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + 7 = -\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} + 7 = \dfrac{15}{2}$. So the remainder is $\dfrac{15}{2} = 7.5$.

questions.stem_md: When $x^3 - kx^2 + 2x + 3$ is divided by $(x - 2)$, the remainder is $7$. Find $k$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = x^3 - kx^2 + 2x + 3$. By the remainder theorem the remainder is $f(2)$.

$f(2) = 2^3 - k \times 2^2 + 2 \times 2 + 3 = 8 - 4k + 4 + 3 = 15 - 4k$

$15 - 4k = 7$, so $4k = 8$ and $k = 2$.

questions.stem_md: Is $(2x - 3)$ a factor of $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 6$? Justify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 6$; $2x - 3 = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

$f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^3 - 3 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2 + 4 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) - 6 = \dfrac{27}{4} - \dfrac{27}{4} + 6 - 6 = 0$

So, by the factor theorem, $(2x - 3)$ **is** a factor. (Indeed $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 6 = (2x - 3)(x^2 + 2)$.)

questions.stem_md: When $2x^3 + kx^2 - 4x + 1$ is divided by $(2x - 1)$, the remainder is $\dfrac{1}{2}$. Find the value of $k$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 + kx^2 - 4x + 1$; $2x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so the remainder is $f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$.

$f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 + k \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 - 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} + 1 = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{k}{4} - 2 + 1 = \dfrac{k - 3}{4}$

$\dfrac{k - 3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $k - 3 = 2$ and $k = 5$.

$f(-1) = -1 + k - 6 = k - 7$; $g(-1) = 2 - k + 3 = 5 - k$.

questions.stem_md: $(x + 2)$ is a factor of $2x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 2$, and the polynomial leaves a remainder of $6$ when divided by $(x - 1)$. Find $a$ and $b$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 2$.

Factor $(x + 2)$: $f(-2) = -16 + 4a - 2b - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow 2a - b = 9$.

Remainder $6$ on division by $(x - 1)$: $f(1) = 2 + a + b - 2 = 6 \Rightarrow a + b = 6$.

Adding the two equations: $3a = 15$, so $a = 5$ and $b = 1$.

questions.stem_md: When $x^3 + px^2 + qx + 5$ is divided by $(x - 1)$ the remainder is $5$, and when it is divided by $(x + 2)$ the remainder is $11$. Find $p$ and $q$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = x^3 + px^2 + qx + 5$.

$f(1) = 1 + p + q + 5 = 5 \Rightarrow p + q = -1$.

$f(-2) = -8 + 4p - 2q + 5 = 11 \Rightarrow 2p - q = 7$.

Adding: $3p = 6$, so $p = 2$ and $q = -3$.

The polynomial is $x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x + 5$.

questions.stem_md: Show that $(3x + 2)$ is a factor of $3x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x - 2$. Hence factorise the polynomial completely.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = 3x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x - 2$; $3x + 2 = 0$ gives $x = -\dfrac{2}{3}$.

$f\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 3 \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^3 + 2 \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 - 3 \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) - 2 = -\dfrac{8}{9} + \dfrac{8}{9} + 2 - 2 = 0$, so $(3x + 2)$ is a factor.

Grouping the terms:

$3x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x - 2 = x^2(3x + 2) - (3x + 2) = (3x + 2)(x^2 - 1) = (3x + 2)(x - 1)(x + 1)$

questions.stem_md: Find the value of $m$ for which $(x + 3)$ is a factor of $2x^3 + mx^2 - 11x - 6$. For this value of $m$, factorise the polynomial completely.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 + mx^2 - 11x - 6$. By the factor theorem, $f(-3) = 0$:

$f(-3) = 2 \times (-3)^3 + m \times (-3)^2 - 11 \times (-3) - 6 = -54 + 9m + 33 - 6 = 9m - 27$

$9m - 27 = 0$, so $m = 3$.

Dividing by $(x + 3)$ and factorising the quotient:

$2x^3 + 3x^2 - 11x - 6 = (x + 3)(2x^2 - 3x - 2) = (x + 3)(2x + 1)(x - 2)$

Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) Find the remainder when $x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x + 7$ is divided by $(x - 3)$.

(b) Show that $(x + 1)$ is a factor of $2x^3 - x^2 - 2x + 1$.

(c) Hence factorise $2x^3 - x^2 - 2x + 1$ completely.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Let $f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x + 7$. By the remainder theorem the remainder is $f(3)$:

$f(3) = 3^3 + 2 \times 3^2 - 5 \times 3 + 7 = 27 + 18 - 15 + 7 = 37$. The remainder is $37$.

**(b)** Let $g(x) = 2x^3 - x^2 - 2x + 1$.

$g(-1) = 2 \times (-1)^3 - (-1)^2 - 2 \times (-1) + 1 = -2 - 1 + 2 + 1 = 0$, so $(x + 1)$ is a factor by the factor theorem.

**(c)** Dividing by $(x + 1)$: $2x^3 - x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x + 1)(2x^2 - 3x + 1)$.

Splitting the middle term, $2x^2 - 3x + 1 = (2x - 1)(x - 1)$.

So $2x^3 - x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x + 1)(2x - 1)(x - 1)$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) evaluates at x = 3; part (b) shows the value at x = −1 is zero; part (c) divides by x + 1 and factorises the quadratic quotient.

questions.stem_md:

(a) Find the remainder when $x^3 - 6x^2 + 2x - 4$ is divided by $(1 - 2x)$.

(b) $g(x) = x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 15$ has $(x - 3)$ as a factor and leaves a remainder of $-24$ when divided by $(x - 1)$. Find $a$ and $b$.

(c) Factorise $g(x)$ completely.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $1 - 2x = 0$ gives $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

$f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 - 6 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 + 2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) - 4 = \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{3}{2} + 1 - 4 = -\dfrac{35}{8}$. The remainder is $-\dfrac{35}{8}$.

**(b)** $g(3) = 27 + 9a + 3b - 15 = 0 \Rightarrow 3a + b = -4$.

$g(1) = 1 + a + b - 15 = -24 \Rightarrow a + b = -10$.

Subtracting: $2a = 6$, so $a = 3$ and $b = -13$.

**(c)** $g(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 - 13x - 15$, and $(x - 3)$ is a factor. Dividing:

$x^3 + 3x^2 - 13x - 15 = (x - 3)(x^2 + 6x + 5) = (x - 3)(x + 5)(x + 1)$

$x^2 + 6x + 5 = (x + 5)(x + 1)$

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) Show that $(x - 2)$ is a factor of $f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x - 10$.

(b) Show that $f(x)$ has no other linear factor.

(c) $g(x) = x^3 + mx^2 + nx - 10$ is exactly divisible by $x^2 - x - 2$. Find $m$ and $n$, and the third factor of $g(x)$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $f(2) = 2^3 - 2 \times 2^2 + 5 \times 2 - 10 = 8 - 8 + 10 - 10 = 0$, so $(x - 2)$ is a factor.

**(b)** Grouping: $x^3 - 2x^2 + 5x - 10 = x^2(x - 2) + 5(x - 2) = (x - 2)(x^2 + 5)$.

For every real $x$, $x^2 + 5 \ge 5$, so $x^2 + 5$ is never zero and has no linear factor. Hence $(x - 2)$ is the only linear factor of $f(x)$.

**(c)** $x^2 - x - 2 = (x - 2)(x + 1)$, so $(x - 2)$ and $(x + 1)$ are both factors of $g(x)$:

$g(2) = 8 + 4m + 2n - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow 2m + n = 1$.

$g(-1) = -1 + m - n - 10 = 0 \Rightarrow m - n = 11$.

Adding: $3m = 12$, so $m = 4$ and $n = -7$.

Then $x^3 + 4x^2 - 7x - 10 = (x^2 - x - 2)(x + 5) = (x - 2)(x + 1)(x + 5)$: the third factor is $(x + 5)$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) shows f(2) = 0; part (b) groups the terms and shows the quadratic factor is always positive; part (c) factorises the divisor and uses the factor theorem twice.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined carton maker designs a box whose volume, in cm³, is $V(x) = x^3 + 5x^2 + 2x - 8$ for a design number $x > 1$. Show all working.

(a) Show that $(x - 1)$ is a factor of $V(x)$.

(b) Factorise $V(x)$ completely, so that each factor can be the length of one edge of the box.

(c) For $x = 6$, find the three edges and the volume of the box. Find the remainder when $V(x)$ is divided by $(x - 6)$, and explain why it equals the volume.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The coefficients add up to $1 + 5 + 2 - 8 = 0$: $V(1) = 1^3 + 5 \times 1^2 + 2 \times 1 - 8 = 1 + 5 + 2 - 8 = 0$, so $(x - 1)$ is a factor.

**(b)** Dividing by $(x - 1)$: $x^3 + 5x^2 + 2x - 8 = (x - 1)(x^2 + 6x + 8) = (x - 1)(x + 4)(x + 2)$.

$x^2 + 6x + 8 = (x + 4)(x + 2)$. The edges are $(x - 1)$ cm, $(x + 2)$ cm and $(x + 4)$ cm.

**(c)** At $x = 6$ the edges are $5$ cm, $8$ cm and $10$ cm, so the volume is $5 \times 8 \times 10 = 400$ cm³.

By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x - 6)$ is $V(6) = 6^3 + 5 \times 6^2 + 2 \times 6 - 8 = 216 + 180 + 12 - 8 = 400$.

It equals the volume because both are the value of $V(x)$ at $x = 6$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) uses the sum of the coefficients; part (b) divides by x − 1 and factorises the quotient; part (c) substitutes 6 in each factor and links the remainder theorem to the value of V.
